name: Visual Question Answering: Datasets, Algorithms, and Future Challenges
description: A review paper that critically examines the current state of visual question answering (VQA) in terms of problem formulation, existing datasets, evaluation metrics, and algorithms, with emphasis on limitations of current datasets and future directions.
creator: Kushal Kafle and Christopher Kanan
citeAs: Kafle, K. and Kanan, C. Visual Question Answering: Datasets, Algorithms, and Future Challenges.
rai:dataCollection: This paper is a review of existing VQA datasets rather than a dataset paper. It describes data collection procedures used by several VQA datasets. Examples explicitly described include: COCO-QA created QA pairs from COCO image captions using an NLP algorithm; COCO-VQA used Amazon Mechanical Turk workers to generate questions by asking them to 'Stump a smart robot,' with a separate pool of workers generating answers; Visual Genome used two distinct modes of data collection, free-form questions and region-specific prompting using descriptive bounding-box annotations; Visual7W used plausible multiple-choice answers collected by prompting annotators to answer without seeing the image; FM-IQA contains human generated questions and answers and was originally collected in Chinese with English translations made available.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Software Collection, Experiments
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: For FM-IQA, the authors state: 'We were unable to retrieve the English version of the dataset from provided download link.'
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The reviewed datasets draw images from existing sources including Microsoft COCO, NYU-DepthV2, Flickr100M/YFCC100M, and synthetic cartoon scenes. COCO-QA derives QA pairs from COCO captions. Visual Genome uses images occurring in both YFCC100M and COCO. SYNTH-VQA uses synthetic cartoon scenes made from object, animal, and human cartoon models.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Beginning in 2014, five major datasets for VQA have been publicly released.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: COCO-QA QA pairs are automatically derived from captions using an NLP algorithm; longer sentences are broken into smaller chunks for ease of processing. The VQA Dataset multiple-choice format adds 18 answer choices composed of the correct answer, plausible answers, popular answers, and random answers. Visual7W constructs multiple-choice options using plausible answers and plausible bounding boxes.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For COCO-QA, longer caption sentences are broken into smaller chunks before question generation. For FM-IQA, English translations were made available for data originally collected in Chinese. In the authors' own experiments described in the review, toy datasets were created from the validation split of COCO using annotations to determine whether an image contained a person and by asking controlled question variations.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The paper describes annotation protocols for reviewed datasets. COCO-VQA has three questions per image and ten answers per question; AMT workers generated questions by being asked to 'Stump a smart robot,' and a separate pool of workers generated answers. Visual Genome used free-form question asking and region-specific prompting based on annotated image regions. Visual7W collected plausible answers by prompting annotators to answer without seeing the image; for pointing questions, plausible bounding boxes were used as choices. DAQUAR-consensus collected additional ground truth answers for consensus evaluation. FM-IQA contains human generated questions and answers.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper discusses substantial annotator disagreement and consensus-based labeling. For The VQA Dataset, ten answers per question are used with a consensus-based evaluation metric. Inter-human agreement on COCO-VQA is about 83.3%, and agreement is especially poor for 'Why' questions, with over 59% having fewer than three annotators giving exactly the same answer. The paper notes that some questions have opposing answers from annotators, including more than 13% of yes/no answers having both 'yes' and 'no' repeated by more than three annotators. DAQUAR-consensus proposed average consensus and min consensus for combining multiple human answers.
rai:annotationsPerItem: COCO-VQA: 10 answers per question; DAQUAR-consensus: average of 5 human annotated ground truth answers per question; Visual7W multiple-choice: 4 possible answers; COCO-VQA multiple-choice: 18 choices.
rai:annotatorDemographics: For SYNTH-VQA, the synthetic human cartoon models span different age, gender, and races to provide variation in appearance.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm for COCO-QA question-answer generation; word2vec; ResNet classifier for bounding box labels in FDA; external natural language parser in NMN.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The paper explicitly mentions age, gender, and races for synthetic human cartoon models in SYNTH-VQA.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that the most immediate application of VQA is as an aid to blind and visually impaired individuals, enabling them to get information about images on the web and in the real world. It also discusses broader uses for improving human-computer interaction and image retrieval.
rai:dataBiases: The paper repeatedly discusses strong biases in existing VQA datasets. It states that many COCO-VQA questions can be accurately answered without using the image due to language biases, with image-blind algorithms achieving 49.6% accuracy using the question alone. It notes that yes/no answers span about 38% of COCO-VQA questions and almost 59% of them are answered with 'yes.' It also states that Visual Genome free-form questioning can promote bias in the kinds of questions asked, and that SHAPES is balanced and free of bias. The paper concludes that language bias critically affects performance and that current VQA systems are more dependent on the question than the image content.
rai:dataLimitations: The paper identifies many limitations across reviewed datasets: DAQUAR is too small, contains exclusively indoor scenes, and has cluttered, low-resolution, difficult images; COCO-QA contains awkward, grammatically incorrect, and sometimes unintelligible automatically generated questions and only four question types; COCO-VQA contains subjective, opinion-seeking, explanatory, and descriptive questions without single objective answers, strong language bias, and inflated evaluation due to consensus scoring; FM-IQA allows full-sentence answers, making automatic evaluation intractable; Visual Genome has high answer diversity and long-tailed distributions that make open-ended evaluation challenging; multiple-choice evaluation can let systems exploit answer biases instead of solving VQA. The paper states that existing VQA benchmarks are not sufficient to evaluate whether an algorithm has 'solved' VQA.
rai:dataUseCases: The reviewed datasets are used to train and evaluate VQA systems. The paper explicitly states that these datasets enable VQA systems to be trained and evaluated. It discusses use for open-ended and multiple-choice evaluation, benchmarking algorithms, and assessing question-answering performance across datasets. It also recommends that future datasets be used with more nuanced benchmarking, such as mean per-question type performance rather than overall accuracy.
